title: FPIs Pivot to Consumer Services and Healthcare in July, Dump Capital Goods
excerpt: Foreign portfolio investors pumped ₹20,199 crore into Indian equities in July, reversing June's ₹49,341 crore selloff — but the money went almost entirely into consumption and healthcare while cyclical sectors saw heavy outflows.
body:
• FPIs turned net buyers in July 2026 with ₹20,199 crore in inflows, reversing June's ₹49,341 crore selloff after four straight months of heavy outflows
  • Consumer services (₹10,201 crore), healthcare (₹7,755 crore), and consumer durables (₹7,342 crore) attracted 125% of total equity inflows — funded by selling cyclicals
  • Capital goods lost ₹6,275 crore, telecom shed ₹5,725 crore, and automobiles saw ₹4,564 crore exit, signalling defensive repositioning
  • Vallum Capital's analysis: "Foreign money is backing India's household, not India's capex cycle" — a bet on consumption over infrastructure

Foreign portfolio investors reversed course in July, pumping ₹20,199 crore into Indian equities after pulling out ₹49,341 crore in June. But the money did not flow back evenly. FPIs concentrated their buying almost entirely in consumer services, healthcare, and consumer durables — sectors tied to domestic consumption — while simultaneously dumping capital goods, telecom, and automobiles. The rotation marks a clear shift in thesis: foreign money is betting on Indian households, not India's infrastructure push.

Where the Money Went

A report from Vallum Capital broke down the July flows. Consumer services attracted ₹10,201 crore, making it the single largest recipient of FPI money during the month. Healthcare followed with ₹7,755 crore, and consumer durables drew ₹7,342 crore. Together, these three sectors absorbed ₹25,298 crore — 125% of total equity inflows — meaning FPIs funded these purchases by selling other holdings.

The buying pattern extended into the first half of July as well. NSDL data showed consumer services leading sectoral inflows during July 1-15, followed by metals and mining (₹5,993 crore) and healthcare (₹4,101 crore). Financial services received ₹1,975 crore in the first half, extending a reversal that began in late June after months of heavy selling. IT stocks saw marginal buying of ₹60 crore — a potentially significant turn after FPIs had sold over ₹34,000 crore of IT shares in 2026 through June.

"Foreign money is backing India's household, not India's capex cycle. FPIs are buying discretionary consumption and healthcare, sectors where earnings visibility is higher and global macro risks matter less."

— Vallum Capital, July sectoral analysis

Where the Money Left

The outflows tell an equally clear story. Capital goods lost ₹6,275 crore, telecom shed ₹5,725 crore, and automobiles saw ₹4,564 crore exit. These are cyclical, capex-linked sectors that depend on government spending, infrastructure contracts, and industrial demand — precisely the segments where global macro uncertainty creates the most earnings risk.

The pattern signals defensive repositioning rather than a broad India bull call. FPIs are choosing sectors where earnings growth is visible and less sensitive to oil prices, interest rate movements, or geopolitical disruptions. Healthcare and consumer services offer that profile; capital goods and telecom do not.

The Consumption Thesis

The sectoral rotation has a fundamental foundation. Private final consumption expenditure grew 7.1% in the last quarter of FY26. India's Retailers Association reported retail growth of 10% in March and 9% in February. For the full year, private consumption rose 7.7% in FY26, up from 5.8% the previous year — a structural strengthening of household spending, particularly in discretionary categories like retail, travel, hospitality, and services.

The share of private final consumption in India's GDP rose to 61.5% in FY26, making the consumer sector the economy's center of gravity. This shift has not gone unnoticed by global allocators. The Vallum Capital report noted that the sectoral rotation mirrors a global trend toward domestic demand over industrial capex.

Context: The Reversal

July's buying came after four consecutive months of heavy FPI selling: ₹1,17,775 crore in March, ₹60,847 crore in April, ₹32,963 crore in May, and ₹49,340 crore in June. The selling was driven by rising global risk aversion following the US-Iran conflict, surging crude oil prices, and a rotation into AI-linked stocks in developed markets.

"The biggest highlight of this period is that after months of consistent selling in IT, FIIs have turned marginal buyers, suggesting the sector may have bottomed out."

— Apurva Sheth, Head of Research, Samco Securities

Goldman Sachs has noted that foreign investor positioning in Indian equities remains close to multi-year lows, leaving room for global funds to rebuild exposure. The brokerage said recent inflows reflect not just improving sentiment but a positioning trade as investors gradually increase their India allocations from depressed levels.

For Indian markets, the July data carries a mixed message. FPIs are returning, but selectively — and their bets suggest more confidence in India's consumer story than in its infrastructure ambitions. Whether the rotation sustains into August will depend on earnings delivery in these consumption sectors and the trajectory of global risk appetite.
nri_angle: NRI investors can track FPI sectoral flows as a signal for where institutional money sees the strongest earnings visibility in India's evolving market.
author: Diaspora Desk
